about: This prayer is called the embolism, from the Greek word for an insertion: it is slipped in between the Lord's Prayer and the Communion, and it does one thing only — it takes the petition the server has just made, líbera nos a malo, and opens it out. The one evil becomes all evils, and the evils are given three tenses: past, present, and still to come. Its ending is said over the breaking of the Host: the Host is divided in two at Fílium tuum, a small particle is broken from the left-hand half at Qui tecum vivit et regnat, and only the last four words are raised to a voice the church can hear.

s01.narrative: The priest takes the paten between his first and middle fingers, holds it upright over the altar, and says the prayer secretly.

s02.translation: Deliver us, we beseech Thee, O Lord, from all evils, past, present and to come: and by the intercession of the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, with Thy blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and Andrew, and all the Saints,

s03.narrative: The priest signs himself with the paten, from forehead to breast.

s04.translation: graciously grant peace in our days:

s06.translation: that, upheld by the help of Thy mercy, we may be always free from sin and safe from all disquiet.

s07.narrative: The priest slips the paten under the Host, uncovers the chalice, genuflects, rises, takes the Host, and holding it over the chalice with both hands breaks it in two.

s08.translation: Through the same Jesus Christ our Lord, Thy Son.

s09.narrative: The priest lays the right-hand half on the paten, and from the half left in his hand breaks off a small particle.

s10.translation: Who liveth and reigneth with Thee in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God.

s11.narrative: The priest joins the left-hand half to the half on the paten, holds the small particle over the chalice, and now says or sings aloud.

w001.function: The same imperative the server has just said in the Lord's Prayer; the whole prayer grows out of it.

w003.function: A parenthesis dropped into the sentence, as elsewhere in the Roman prayers; it takes no object of its own here.

w006.function: Agrees with “malis” (w007): the single evil of the petition becomes every evil.

w007.function: Neuter — evils, things that are evil, not evil men; the three adjectives that follow all take this gender.

w008.function: First of three adjectives, all agreeing with “malis” (w007), and all treated by the dictionaries as adjectives in their own right rather than as participles still doing verbal work.

w011.function: Past, present and future close the list: no evil of any time is left outside the petition.

w013.function: Ablative absolute with “Vírgine” (w018): while she intercedes. The construction hangs free of the main clause, which is why English needs “by the intercession of”.

w017.function: Not loose emphasis but part of the title: semper Virgo, ever-Virgin.

w019.function: Depends on “Genetríce” (w020), not on Vírgine: Mother of God, the title defined at Ephesus in 431.

w020.function: In apposition to “Vírgine” (w018). The word means specifically she who bears, a mother by childbearing.

w029.function: Atque joins more tightly than et and gives what follows a slight lift: and Andrew besides.

w032.function: Masculine here, agreeing with “Sanctis” (w033) — the saints, not the evils that the identical “ómnibus” (w006) qualifies.

w033.function: An adjective used as a noun: the holy ones.

w034.function: The verb of its own clause — beside the imperative “Líbera” (w001) — held back until all the intercession has been named: everything since the evils was leading here.

w035.function: An adjective agreeing with the unstated Thou, not an adverb: grant, being favourable. Latin describes the giver where English describes the giving.

w040.function: The comma after ut marks an interruption: the phrase about mercy is wedged between the conjunction and its verb “simus” (w048).

w041.function: Ablative of means with “adiúti” (w044). Ops has no nominative singular in use, so this is one of the three forms the singular has.

w044.function: A participle agreeing with the unstated subject of “simus” (w048) — us.

w045.function: The first half of an et… et… pair with “et” (w051): both free from sin and safe from disquiet.

w048.function: The verb the whole ut clause was waiting for; it governs both “líberi” (w050) and “secúri” (w055).

w050.function: Predicate with “simus” (w048): free from sin — the guilt taken away.

w054.function: Outward disorder and inward agitation at once; the prayer asks peace for the days and quiet for the soul in one breath.

w055.function: The second predicate with “simus” (w048), and the sharper of the pair: freed from sin, and past fearing it.

w057.function: Eúndem wants to point back — but Iesus Christus is not named earlier in this prayer, and the opening “Dómine” reads as the Father. This is a known knot of the embolism, and the word carries the disputed flag.

w062.function: In apposition to “Christum” (w061) and addressed to the Father: through Thy Son. The Host is broken in two on these words.

w065.function: The preposition cum has fused onto the end of the pronoun, as it always does with te, me, se and nobis.

w073.function: Nominative, standing with the two verbs, not an address: He lives and reigns as God. A particle is broken from the Host on these words.

w077.function: A Hebrew way of saying “for ever” carried into Latin word for word: the ages of the ages.
